expectedText:
DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP DISSOLUTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION OF PARTNERS AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Domestic Partnership Dissolution — Information Sheet concerns the registered domestic partnership of Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan, who registered as domestic partners in California on June 1, 2018. It is prepared for background use in connection with the possible filing of a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the California Secretary of State, or a petition for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of the domestic partnership in the Superior Court of California, County of San Francisco County. This information sheet describes California's statutory framework for ending a registered domestic partnership — the administrative and judicial paths, the same-as-marriage standards that apply to the judicial path, and the community-property default — as background for that filing. It is not itself a Notice of Termination or a court filing, and completing it does not terminate, dissolve, or otherwise change the legal status of the domestic partnership of Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan. Only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that.

ADMINISTRATIVE TERMINATION — ELIGIBILITY FOR THE SECRETARY OF STATE'S NOTICE OF TERMINATION
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that California law allows a registered domestic partnership to be terminated without any court dissolution proceeding, by filing a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State, but only if all of the following conditions exist at the time of filing: the Notice is signed by both registered domestic partners; there are no children of the relationship, born or adopted before or after registration, and neither partner knows themselves to be pregnant; the partnership is not more than five years in duration; neither partner has any interest in real property, subject to a narrow exception for a short-term residential lease that includes no purchase option and ends within a year of filing; neither partner has unpaid obligations, or the partners' community-property assets do not exceed, the statutory dollar thresholds set by Family Code Section 2400 (thresholds that are periodically adjusted and are not restated here); the partners have executed an agreement dividing their community-property assets and liabilities; both partners waive any right to support from the other; both partners have read and understand the Secretary of State's brochure describing the requirements, nature, and effect of terminating a domestic partnership; and both partners desire the termination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A registered domestic partnership may be terminated without filing a proceeding for dissolution of domestic partnership by the filing of a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this section, provided that all of the following conditions exist at the time of the filing: (1) The Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership is signed by both registered domestic partners. (2) There are no children of the relationship of the parties born before or after registration of the domestic partnership or adopted by the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, and neither of the registered domestic partners, to their knowledge, is pregnant. (3) The registered domestic partnership is not more than five years in duration. (4) Neither party has any interest in real property wherever situated, with the exception of the lease of a residence occupied by either party which satisfies the following requirements: (A) The lease does not include an option to purchase. (B) The lease terminates within one year from the date of filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership. (5) There are no unpaid obligations in excess of the amount described in paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, incurred by either or both of the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, excluding the amount of any unpaid obligation with respect to an automobile. (6) The total fair market value of community property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, including any deferred compensation or retirement plan, is less than the amount described in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, and neither party has separate property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, in excess of that amount. (7) The parties have executed an agreement setting forth the division of assets and the assumption of liabilities of the community property, and have executed any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other evidence of transfer necessary to effectuate the agreement. (8) The parties waive any rights to support by the other domestic partner. (9) The parties have read and understand a brochure prepared by the Secretary of State describing the requirements, nature, and effect of terminating a domestic partnership. (10) Both parties desire that the domestic partnership be terminated."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299(a) (California Legislative Information text), the ten conditions for administrative termination by Notice of Termination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 299(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. The specific current dollar thresholds referenced by Family Code Section 2400 are indexed and adjusted by the Judicial Council roughly every two years and were not independently re-verified as of any particular current date; this clause states only that such thresholds exist and are cross-referenced, not their present dollar amounts.

EFFECTIVE DATE, REVOCATION, AND COURT CHALLENGE OF AN ADMINISTRATIVE TERMINATION
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that filing a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State does not end the partnership immediately: termination becomes effective six months after the date of filing, unless either partner files a notice of revocation with the Secretary of State and mails a copy of it to the other partner before that date. Once effective, the termination is treated for all purposes as the entry of a judgment of dissolution of the domestic partnership. Terminating a partnership this way does not bar either partner from later asking the superior court to set the termination aside and declare it null and void, on proof that the partners did not actually meet the eligibility conditions at the time of filing, or on a showing of fraud, duress, mistake, or another ground recognized at law or in equity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) The registered domestic partnership shall be terminated effective six months after the date of filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this section, provided that neither party has, before that date, filed with the Secretary of State a notice of revocation of the termination of domestic partnership, in the form and content as shall be prescribed by the Secretary of State, and sent to the other party a copy of the notice of revocation by first-class mail, postage prepaid, at the other party’s last known address. The effect of termination of a domestic partnership pursuant to this section shall be the same as, and shall be treated for all purposes as, the entry of a judgment of dissolution of a domestic partnership. (c) The termination of a domestic partnership pursuant to subdivision (b) does not prejudice nor bar the rights of either of the parties to institute an action in the superior court to set aside the termination for fraud, duress, mistake, or any other ground recognized at law or in equity. A court may set aside the termination of domestic partnership and declare the termination of the domestic partnership null and void upon proof that the parties did not meet the requirements of subdivision (a) at the time of the filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), the six-month effective date, revocation procedure, and grounds to set aside the termination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.)

This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory section, two contiguous subsections (§ 299(b)-(c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

JUDICIAL DISSOLUTION FOR PARTNERSHIPS THAT DON'T QUALIFY — SAME PROCEDURES AS MARRIAGE, PLUS ONE ADDED EXCEPTION
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that a domestic partnership that does not meet every condition for administrative termination can be ended only through a proceeding in California Superior Court, which has jurisdiction over the dissolution, nullity, and legal separation of registered domestic partnerships. Except as provided for administrative termination, that judicial proceeding follows the same procedures, and the partners possess the same rights, protections, and benefits, and are subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties, as apply respectively to the dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage. California law adds one further, partnership-specific rule on top of that equivalence: because a domestic partner's consent to it is built into the Declaration of Domestic Partnership filed at registration, a proceeding to dissolve, void, or legally separate a domestic partnership registered in California may be filed in California's superior courts even if, at the time of filing, neither partner resides in or is domiciled in California — a jurisdictional allowance that does not depend on either partner's sex or on the marriage-specific residency exception that otherwise applies to some marriage-dissolution proceedings under California law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(d) The superior courts shall have jurisdiction over all proceedings relating to the dissolution of domestic partnerships, nullity of domestic partnerships, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership. The dissolution of a domestic partnership, nullity of a domestic partnership, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership shall follow the same procedures, and the partners shall possess the same rights, protections, and benefits, and be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties, as apply to the dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, and legal separation of spouses in a marriage, respectively, except as provided in subdivision (a), and except that, in accordance with the consent acknowledged by domestic partners in the Declaration of Domestic Partnership form, proceedings for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a domestic partnership registered in this state may be filed in the superior courts of this state even if neither domestic partner is a resident of, or maintains a domicile in, the state at the time the proceedings are filed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299(d) (California Legislative Information text), the same-procedures rule for judicial dissolution and its added jurisdictional exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.)

This is a single statutory subsection (§ 299(d)); no additional independent source was found for this. The comparison drawn here to marriage's ordinary residency requirement is general background only, drawn from this corpus's own separately and independently verified citation to Family Code § 2320 in its Petition for Dissolution of Marriage document (clause dissolution_residency_requirement); § 2320 was not independently re-fetched for this document, and no citation to it is included here.

EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE CURRENT TERMINATION RULES, AND A PRE-2005 TRANSITION RULE
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that the version of Family Code Section 299 described in this document — including the five-year duration limit and the other conditions for administrative termination — took its current form through a 2010 amendment that became effective January 1, 2011, and applies to terminations filed on or after that date. Separately, California law carries a narrow transition rule for partnerships registered before January 1, 2005: for those partnerships, an agreement between the partners intended to be governed by California's premarital-agreement statutes, and complying with those statutes apart from its effective date, remains enforceable under those statutes if it was fully executed and in force by June 30, 2005 — even though it was necessarily signed before the partnership's registration rather than before a marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(Amended by Stats. 2010, Ch. 397, Sec. 1. (AB 2700) Effective January 1, 2011.)"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 299, Legislative History Note (California Legislative Information text), the effective date of the current administrative-termination criteria (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=299.)
  "(2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), for domestic partnerships registered with the state before January 1, 2005, an agreement between the domestic partners that the partners intend to be governed by the requirements set forth in Sections 1600 to 1620, inclusive, and which complies with those sections, except for the agreement’s effective date, shall be enforceable as provided by Sections 1600 to 1620, inclusive, if that agreement was fully executed and in force as of June 30, 2005."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(k)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the pre-2005-registration premarital-agreement transition rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.5.)

This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code provisions — § 299's own legislative history note and § 297.5(k)(2) — not subsections of the same section, so each is independent of the other. This clause does not address whether, or how, the current five-year duration limit applied to partnerships that had already exceeded five years' duration as of the 2011 effective date; that transitional question was not researched here.

SAME RIGHTS AND DUTIES AS SPOUSES — DURING THE PARTNERSHIP AND AFTER
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that, under California law, registered domestic partners have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and are subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law — whether arising from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other source of law — as are granted to and imposed upon spouses, and that this same-treatment rule continues in parallel form for former registered domestic partners once a partnership ends, matching how the law treats former spouses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Registered domestic partners shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law, whether they derive from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other provisions or sources of law, as are granted to and imposed upon spouses. (b) Former registered domestic partners shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law, whether they derive from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other provisions or sources of law, as are granted to and imposed upon former spouses."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the same-rights-and-duties statute, for current and former partners (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.5.)

This is a single statutory section, two contiguous subsections (§ 297.5(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

STANDARDS GOVERNING A PARTNER'S RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS REGARDING A CHILD
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that California law makes a registered domestic partner's rights and obligations with respect to a child of either partner the same as a spouse's rights and obligations, and makes a former or surviving registered domestic partner's rights and obligations with respect to such a child the same as a former or surviving spouse's — so that the custody and child-related support standards applied on the dissolution of a marriage with children apply in the same way to the dissolution of a domestic partnership with children, rather than under a separate, partnership-specific standard.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(d) The rights and obligations of registered domestic partners with respect to a child of either of them shall be the same as those of spouses. The rights and obligations of former or surviving registered domestic partners with respect to a child of either of them shall be the same as those of former or surviving spouses."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), the same rights-and-obligations rule regarding a partner's or former partner's children (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for ending a registered domestic partnership — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific partnership. This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(d)); no additional independent source was found for this. This clause states that the same legal standards apply; it does not restate the substance of California's child custody or child support statutes themselves, which this document does not otherwise cover.

COMMUNITY PROPERTY DIVISION AND SPOUSAL SUPPORT — THE MARITAL DEFAULT, APPLIED THROUGH THE REGISTRATION DATE
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that California law ties community-property division and support rules for a domestic partnership to the date the partnership was registered, in the same way those rules turn on the date of marriage for spouses: for community property, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, and either partner's right to seek support from the other after dissolution, any statute referring to "the date of a marriage" is read to mean the date of registration of the domestic partnership. Because a judicial dissolution of a domestic partnership otherwise follows the same procedures as a marital dissolution, the community-property default a court applies absent the partners' own written agreement or oral stipulation in open court — dividing the community estate equally — applies to a domestic partnership's community estate in the same way it applies to a marriage's, even though that default rule's own text refers only to "dissolution of marriage" and "legal separation," not to domestic partnerships by name.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(k) (1) For purposes of the statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, and any other provision or source of law governing the rights, protections, and benefits, and the responsibilities, obligations, and duties of registered domestic partners in this state, as effectuated by this section, with respect to community property, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, the right in particular circumstances of either partner to seek financial support from the other following the dissolution of the partnership, and other rights and duties as between the partners concerning ownership of property, any reference to the date of a marriage shall be deemed to refer to the date of registration of a domestic partnership with the state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(k)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the registration-date-as-marriage-date rule for property and support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.5.)
  "2550. Except upon the written agreement of the parties, or on oral stipulation of the parties in open court, or as otherwise provided in this division, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text), the equal-division default a court applies absent a settlement agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2550.)

This document is informational only: it does not itself terminate any partnership or resolve any dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation matter; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 297.5(k)(1) and § 2550), not subsections of the same section, so each is independent of the other. Section 2550 reaches domestic partnership dissolution only indirectly — through § 299(d)'s same-procedures rule and § 297.5(k)(1)'s registration-date-as-marriage-date rule — not because § 2550 itself mentions domestic partnerships; this clause states that chain of cross-reference explicitly rather than assuming it. This clause does not address spousal/partner support amount or duration standards, which this document does not otherwise cover.

ONE EXPRESS STATUTORY CARVE-OUT: LONG-TERM CARE PLAN ELIGIBILITY
Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan state that California's same-rights-and-duties statute contains at least one express, narrow carve-out from the general rule that registered domestic partners are treated the same as spouses: that statute does not apply to modify eligibility for long-term care plans made available under a specific chapter of the Government Code governing long-term care benefits for state employees and annuitants.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(g) No public agency in this state may discriminate against any person or couple on the ground that the person is a registered domestic partner rather than a spouse or that the couple are registered domestic partners rather than spouses, except that nothing in this section applies to modify eligibility for long-term care plans pursuant to Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 21660) of Part 3 of Division 5 of Title 2 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(g) (California Legislative Information text), the express long-term-care-plan-eligibility carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=297.5.)

This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(g)); no additional independent source was found for this. This clause identifies the one express carve-out this document's research located within § 297.5 and § 299 themselves; it is not the product of an exhaustive survey of every other Family Code or Government Code provision, and it does not state whether other, narrower differences between domestic-partner and spousal treatment exist elsewhere in California law.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A NOTICE OF TERMINATION OR A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on October 15, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership filed with the Secretary of State, or a petition filed with the California superior court, and it does not terminate, dissolve, void, or legally separate a domestic partnership; only the Secretary of State's processing of a qualifying Notice of Termination, or a court judgment, can do that.]
